evidence: Vulg. Judic. 16.13: sī … septem crīnēs capitis meī cum līciō plexueris
Catull. 64.283: flōrēs plexī (Lewis & Short s.v. plectō)
terms.comment: The verb plectō is classical but rare, used of garlands (Lucretius, Catullus); of hair we have found it in the Vulgate, where Delilah weaves Samson’s locks into the loom.
terms.grammar: plexus, the participle of plectō, plectere, plexī (plexuī), plexum; to plait the hair is crīnēs plectere

evidence: Plin. NH 21.11: corōna pāctilis, a plaited garland, as against one sewn together (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Morgan–Owens’s phrase, given with a query. Pāctilis is Pliny’s word for a garland plaited of flowers; we have found no ancient name for a plait of hair.

phrases.latin: sī … septem crīnēs capitis meī cum līciō plexueris et clāvum hīs circumligātum terrae fīxeris, īnfirmus erō
phrases.english: if you weave the seven locks of my head into the web, and fasten them round a peg driven into the ground, I shall be weak

sources: Lewis & Short: pactilis · Lewis & Short: plecto
Morgan–Owens, Adumbratio: s.v. braid, pony-tail, etc.
